culture-intro-s1.title: Two visitors at a family dinner in Seoul
culture-intro-s1.html:
Two visitors at one dinner in Seoul, South Korea (invented notes, written by LevlPrep for practice, 2026)

Visitor 1: "Small side dishes sat in the middle of the table, and everyone shared them. No one ate until the grandmother picked up her spoon. I asked my host why, and she said it shows respect for older people. By the second night, I waited too."

Visitor 2: "No one had their own plate, which seemed strange and messy to me. Back home we each get our own plate, and that is simply the correct way to eat. They should learn to do it properly."

culture-intro-s2.title: Two kinds of culture in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania
culture-intro-s2.html:
Lancaster County, Pennsylvania (LevlPrep summary, 2026)

Many Amish families in Lancaster County travel by horse and buggy, wear plain clothing in dark colors, and speak Pennsylvania Dutch, a language that grew from German, at home. Neighbors gather to raise a barn together in a day. These ways are taught by parents and church members and change slowly.

A few miles away, shopping centers hold chain stores and fast-food restaurants that look the same as ones in Texas or Ohio. Teenagers there stream the same songs and shows as teenagers across the country, and the most popular ones change every few months.

cultural-patterns-s2.title: Murals in Pilsen, Chicago
cultural-patterns-s2.html:
Pilsen, Chicago (LevlPrep summary, 2026)

Pilsen, on the Lower West Side of Chicago, Illinois, has been home to a large Mexican American community since the mid-1900s. Artists from the neighborhood have painted dozens of murals on walls, viaducts and schools. Many show Aztec symbols, Mexican history, local families and the Virgin of Guadalupe. The National Museum of Mexican Art (then called the Mexican Fine Arts Center Museum) opened in Pilsen in 1987. Each year, residents gather for street festivals with music and food from Mexico. Many residents say the murals tell visitors "this is our neighborhood."

diffusion-types-s2.title: Sequoyah and the Cherokee syllabary
diffusion-types-s2.html:
Sequoyah and the Cherokee syllabary (LevlPrep summary, 2026)

Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith born about 1770, could not read English, but he watched English speakers send messages on paper. He became convinced that the Cherokee language could be written too. By 1821 he had finished a syllabary: a set of 86 symbols, each standing for a syllable of spoken Cherokee rather than a single sound. Some symbols look like Latin letters, but they stand for completely different sounds. Within a few years many Cherokee people could read and write, and in 1828 the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper began printing in Cherokee and English.

diffusion-history-s1.title: Swahili, a language of East African ports
diffusion-history-s1.html:
Swahili on the East African coast (LevlPrep summary, 2026)

For more than a thousand years, ports such as Kilwa, Mombasa and Zanzibar traded across the Indian Ocean with merchants from Arabia, Persia and India. Swahili, a Bantu language of the coast, took in many Arabic words through this trade; its name comes from an Arabic word for "coasts." In the 1800s, trading caravans carried goods and Swahili inland toward the Great Lakes. Traders, porters and farmers who spoke different home languages used Swahili to bargain with each other. Kenya and Tanzania later made Swahili a national language, and people across East Africa speak it as a second language.

diffusion-today-s2.title: Reviving te reo Māori in New Zealand
diffusion-today-s2.html:
Te reo Māori in New Zealand (LevlPrep summary, 2026)

Te reo Māori is the language of the Māori, the Indigenous people of New Zealand. For much of the 1900s, schools taught in English and many Māori children were punished for speaking te reo. By the 1970s, studies found that few young Māori spoke it fluently. Māori leaders pushed back. Māori Language Week began in 1975. In 1982, families opened the first kōhanga reo, "language nests" where young children spend the day speaking only te reo. The Māori Language Act of 1987 made te reo an official language of New Zealand, and a Māori television channel began broadcasting in 2004.

diffusion-effects-s1.title: Four cases of cultures meeting
diffusion-effects-s1.html:
Four cases (LevlPrep, 2026; cases 1 and 2 describe invented people, cases 3 and 4 real places)

Case 1. Mai moved from Viet Nam to Houston, Texas, in 2015. She learned English for her job and cheers for the Houston Texans, but she speaks Vietnamese at home and celebrates Tết, the Lunar New Year.

Case 2. The great-grandchildren of Norwegian immigrants to rural Minnesota speak only English. Apart from one holiday dish, they keep no Norwegian customs and think of themselves simply as Americans.

Case 3. In Mexico, the Day of the Dead blends Indigenous traditions of honoring the dead with the Catholic days of All Saints and All Souls, into a festival with altars, marigolds and sugar skulls.

Case 4. In Toronto, Canada, many groups keep their own languages, festivals and neighborhoods side by side. Canada made multiculturalism an official policy in 1971.

place.label: Place
options: Minnesota

why.1: A vague place earns no credit. Name the state.

ass.label: Assimilation example

a newcomer who speaks two languages

a festival that blends two religions
